title: Same Meaning, Different Word
blurb: Understand reference words in a text

steps.html:
Three of the four things people say about the moon are nonsense. The fourth sounds the most like a story and happens to be true. Along the way: the small words — this, that, it, one, such, do so — that hold a text together, and that most readers skip.

  • Work out what a reference word refers back to
  • Use synonyms and antonyms precisely
  • Read for the writer's real position, not the surface claim
  • Write a text that holds together without repeating itself

steps.title: Study the words.
steps.sub: Thirteen items, arranged in opposite pairs. The pairs are the point.

words.def: Real; exactly what it appears to be. Opposite: faked.

Happening by chance, not intended. Opposite: deliberate.

Making you feel low. Opposite: cheerful.
Expression of disapproval, or careful judgement of something. Opposite: praise.
The fact of not being there. Opposite: presence.
The fact of being there. Opposite: absence.
To keep, or to continue to have.

steps.title: The small words that hold a text together
steps.html:
Read this before the texts. You will use it immediately.

Good writing does not repeat a noun phrase every time it is needed. It refers back to it with a small word, and the reader is expected to know which one is meant.

it refers to a specific thing already named. this and that can refer to a thing, but also to a whole idea in the previous sentence: Several studies have failed to find evidence for this.

one replaces a countable noun, so it can be counted and modified: the one nobody repeats, a stiff wire, and one that had been reported.

such means 'of that kind': Such occurrences are coincidence.

do so replaces a whole verb phrase in formal writing: The tilt would wander, and it would do so by a great deal. Compare in doing so, they started the myth.

When you meet one of these, stop and ask what exactly does this stand for? — and answer with the actual words from earlier in the text.

steps.title: Which reference word replaces a whole verb phrase?
steps.why: Do so stands in for the action: the tilt would wander, and it would do so by a great deal.

steps.title: Four things people believe about the moon
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 146 words

There is almost no scientific basis for any of them, and that has never made the slightest difference to how widely they are believed.

The first is that the landings were faked. When the American team reached the surface, they planted a flag; in doing so, they accidentally started the myth, because the flag appeared to move in a wind that could not exist. It was not a deliberate hoax. It was a stiff wire in the fabric, and one that had been reported at the time.

The second is that a supermoon causes tsunamis. The moon does affect the tides, but only slightly. Such occurrences are coincidence.

The third is that a full moon changes how people behave. Several studies have failed to find evidence for this, and their absence from the account is itself the interesting part.

The fourth is genuine, and it is the one nobody repeats.

steps.title: The one that turns out to be true
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 146 words

If the moon disappeared, the Earth would sometimes lie on its side. That sounds like the least plausible of the four claims. It is the only one that is not nonsense.

The moon holds the tilt of the Earth's axis steady. Without that presence, the tilt would wander, and it would do so by a great deal. The result would be extreme temperatures and wildly different lengths of daylight — cheerful summers and depressing winters at the same latitude.

Mars offers the evidence. Its axis has tilted so far in the past that the ice at its poles has slid down towards the equator. Nothing holds it in place.

So three of the four beliefs collapse under any criticism, and the fourth, which sounds the most like a story, retains its scientific standing. That is worth remembering the next time something sounds too strange to be true.

steps.title: Choosing the right one
steps.html:
You have used them for reading. Now use them to stop repeating yourself.

it / they — a thing already named, with no emphasis. The moon affects the tides, but it does so only slightly.

this / these — something near, or the idea just stated, when you are about to say more about it. Several studies failed to find evidence for this.

that / those — something further away, or an idea you are stepping back from. That sounds implausible. A useful rule: this pulls the reader in, that holds the idea at arm's length.

one / ones — a countable noun, and you can put words in front of it: the one nobody repeats, a stiff wire, and one that had been reported. Never use one for an uncountable noun: I need advice — have you got one?

such — 'of the kind just described'. Such occurrences are coincidence.

do so / do that / do it — a whole verb phrase. Do so is the formal choice and is common in writing; do it is neutral.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences from the two texts.

There is no basis for any of them.
Them = the four beliefs.

That has never made the slightest difference.
That = the absence of a basis. A whole idea.

In doing so, they accidentally started the myth.
Do so = plant a flag.

It was a stiff wire, and one that had been reported.
One = a wire.

Such occurrences are coincidence.
= occurrences of that kind.

Several studies have failed to find evidence for this.
This = the claim just made.

Their absence from the popular account is the interesting part.
Their = the studies'.

It is the one nobody repeats.
One = belief.

The tilt would wander, and it would do so by a great deal.
Formal, and it avoids repeating wander.

That is worth remembering.
That = the whole conclusion of the paragraph.

steps.title: Removing a repetition
steps.html:
1. The draft: The moon affects the tides. The moon affects the tides only slightly.
  2. The second sentence repeats a noun and a verb phrase. Replace the noun with it: It affects the tides only slightly.
  3. Now the verb phrase repeats too. Replace it with do so: The moon affects the tides, but it does so only slightly.
  4. Check the reader can find the referent. It = the moon; does so = affects the tides. Both are in the sentence before.
  5. One more: if you wanted to step back from the whole idea, you would write That is worth remembering. — that, not it, because it refers to an idea rather than a thing.

steps.title: You are going to write about something widely believed that is not true.

options.label: A belief about learning or memory
A belief about your country that outsiders hold
A belief you held yourself until recently

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least five reference words, and do not repeat any noun phrase twice.
steps.placeholder: There is almost no evidence for …
steps.html:
• Open with a general statement and a reference word.
  • Give three beliefs, numbered, each in its own short paragraph.
  • Use <i>in doing so</i> or <i>do so</i> at least once.
  • Use <i>such</i> at least once.
  • Close with the true one, using <i>the one</i> and <i>that</i>.

Useful language

  • There is almost no evidence for this, and that has never …
  • The first is that … ; the second is that …
  • In doing so, they …
  • Such claims are …
  • It is the one nobody repeats.
  • That is worth remembering the next time …
steps.modelHtml:
Three things people believe about learning a language

There is almost no evidence for any of them, and that has never stopped anybody repeating them.

The first is that children learn faster than adults. Studies comparing the two under the same conditions find the opposite, and their absence from the popular account is itself revealing.

The second is that you must live in the country. This helps, obviously, but plenty of people move abroad and learn nothing; in doing so they prove that exposure alone does very little.

The third is that some people simply have no ear for languages. Such claims are almost always made by people who stopped after six weeks.

The one nobody repeats is the true one: that the strongest predictor is how many hours you have put in. That is dull, and it is worth remembering the next time somebody tells you they are just not a languages person.
